before.approach: From the Yellow Aster Butte/Tomyhoi Lake trailhead (also called the "Keep Kool" trailhead, ~3,600-3,700 ft) on Twin Lakes Road (FR 3065), start on the well-maintained Yellow Aster Butte Trail (Trail #686). The trail climbs through forest switchbacks and crosses a couple of small seasonal creeks/seep crossings in the first mile — reliable water here early season, less so by late summer. At roughly 2.3-2.5 miles (~5,400 ft) you reach the signed junction with the Tomyhoi Lake Trail, which splits off to the right; stay left/straight, continuing up toward Gold Run Pass (~5,900 ft). From the pass area the trail contours into the Yellow Aster Meadows and a basin of small tarns/lakes at about 5,200-5,600 ft (roughly 2 hours/4 miles from the car at a moderate pace) — this is the last dependable water on route. From the basin, leave the maintained trail and head north/NNW over a broad hump and down to a col around 6,266 ft, then pick up a well-defined, boot-packed climbers' path along the crest of the Tomyhoi Arm ridge. As the ridge narrows above roughly 6,800-7,000 ft, bypass the narrowest sections on broad benches on the north (right) side rather than staying on the crest. The path eventually fades into scree and talus as you approach the toe of the Tomyhoi Glacier; traverse along the top edge of the glacier (minor crevasse hazard depending on year/season — assess before committing) to avoid several rock pinnacles, aiming for a notch/moat below the false summit at about 7,250 ft. This upper section is loose, exposed, and route-finding is not obvious — expect some scrambling and sidehilling on scree and rock benches. Total approach is roughly 6-7 miles and ~3,600-3,800 ft of gain one-way from the trailhead to the base of the summit block, consistent with the ~13-14 mile, ~4,800-5,600 ft round-trip character of this route.

approach_variants.name: Yellow Aster Butte Trail #686 over Gold Run Pass, then the Tomyhoi Arm ridge to the moat below the false summit
approach_variants.notes:
From the Yellow Aster Butte / Tomyhoi Lake trailhead — also called the Keep Kool trailhead, around 3,600-3,700 ft — on Twin Lakes Road (FR-3065), start on Yellow Aster Butte Trail #686. It climbs through forest switchbacks with a couple of seasonal creek crossings in the first mile.

At roughly 2.3-2.5 miles near 5,400 ft the signed Tomyhoi Lake Trail splits off RIGHT. Stay left and continue toward Gold Run Pass near 5,900 ft, then contour into the Yellow Aster Meadows and a basin of small tarns at about 5,200-5,600 ft — roughly two hours and four miles from the car, and the last dependable water.

From the basin leave maintained trail: head north-northwest over a broad hump and down to a col around 6,266 ft, then pick up a well-defined boot-packed climbers' path along the crest of the Tomyhoi Arm.

As the ridge narrows above roughly 6,800-7,000 ft, bypass the narrowest sections on broad benches on the NORTH — right — side rather than staying on the crest. The path fades into scree and talus near the toe of the Tomyhoi Glacier.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. The moat below the false summit opens as the season goes on and is the crux either way
hazards: A rock-and-ice moat at the notch that is the crux of the outing and widens through the season
Glacier-polished slick rock at the snow margin
Minor crevasse hazard traversing the top edge of the Tomyhoi Glacier
Loose, exposed, non-obvious route-finding on scree and rock benches approaching the notch
The descent through the V-slot is the most exposed step of the day and is where parties rope up
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS A MOAT, NOT A LEDGE — THE CLIMBING STARTS WHERE THE GLACIER MEETS THE ROCK AT ABOUT 7,200-7,250 FT, AT A NOTCH IN THE JAGGED RIDGE BELOW THE FALSE SUMMIT. Traverse along the TOP EDGE of the Tomyhoi Glacier to avoid several rock pinnacles, and aim for that notch. Getting into it means a traverse on hard snow around a small moat, and in many years that shallow rock-and-ice moat is the crux of the entire outing.

THE ROCK BY THE GLACIER IS GLACIER-POLISHED AND SLICK, and that is a tactile confirmation you are in the right place as well as a warning. Smooth, scoured rock at the snow margin means you are at the moat.

THERE IS A DOCUMENTED ALTERNATIVE AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING BEFORE YOU COMMIT: drop 100 to 200 ft LOWER and climb a rock finger to reach the same notch. A party that arrives at an open moat it does not like has a published option other than retreat.

GEAR IS GENUINELY DISPUTED HERE and the honest statement is that reports differ: some parties manage the moat traverse with an ice axe alone on firm snow, others want crampons. It opens as the season goes on. Carry for the worse case.

ABOVE THE NOTCH, THE SEQUENCE IS THE CHECK: an exposed traverse around a rib gains the climbable side of the summit block, then roughly 160 ft along the LEFT edge of the ridge, then a ledge crossed WEST to a wide corner where the crux is a short V-shaped SLOT. Third class throughout with that one slot harder. The block looks far worse from the false summit than it climbs — repeatedly, in every account — so an intimidating view from the false summit is not evidence you are off route.

OLD RING PITONS ON THE ROUTE are a reminder this is not a maintained line, not a sign you are on the right one.

pitch_detail.notes: Maintained Yellow Aster Butte/Gold Run Pass Trail to ~5,900 ft, then Yellow Aster Meadows Trail to tarns at ~5,580 ft.
Off-trail NNW over a hump, down to a col at ~6,266 ft, then up the broadening Tomyhoi Arm ridge.
pitch_detail.pitch: Meadows to col and lower ridge

pitch_detail.notes: Bypass the narrowing ridge on broad benches on the north side; traverse the top edge of the Tomyhoi Glacier to avoid rock pinnacles.
Cross a moat between rock and ice to gain a notch; hard snow common, ice axe useful.
Exposed scramble on solid but glacier-polished rock; V-shaped slot near the top is the crux, harder on descent.

before.descent_text: Descend by reversing the Southeast Ridge line of ascent — there is no separate walk-off. From the true summit (7,439 ft), reverse the Class 3 summit block and the exposed ~40-ft gabled section of ridge back to the false summit, then downclimb the short wall to the notch at about 7,250 ft. This downclimb is the most exposed step on the route (big air on both sides), and many parties protect it rather than downclimbing free: previous climbing parties have left an informal rappel/lowering setup at the notch — a sling around a natural rock horn, not a bolted or fixed-chain anchor — good for one short (~15-20 ft) rappel or a doubled-rope lower/handline through the Class 3.5 slot. Inspect and back up any in-place tat before trusting it, or build your own natural anchor; a single 30m or longer rope doubled is plenty. Many parties skip the rappel entirely and instead downclimb this slot with a simple rope belay from above. Below the notch, reverse the traverse across the small snow/ice moat (can be firm or icy in morning conditions — an ice axe is worth carrying), continue back along the glacier's top edge and the north-side benches around the pinnacles, drop to the 6,266-ft col, climb back over the hump, and descend into the Yellow Aster Basin to rejoin the maintained trail. From there it's a straightforward but long descent back down through Gold Run Pass and the Yellow Aster Butte Trail to the trailhead; parties moving at a moderate pace should expect the descent to take nearly as long as the ascent (trip reports cite ~5 hours down), and finishing the lower trail by headlamp is common if the party is not fast.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Yellow Aster Butte/Tomyhoi Lake trailhead (also called the "Keep Kool" trailhead, ~3,600-3,700 ft) on Twin Lakes Road (FR 3065), start on the well-maintained Yellow Aster Butte Trail (Trail #686).

itinerary.cal: Best conditions June-September; snow at the moat traverse is firmest early in the day, so an early (pre-dawn to 8 AM) start is recommended.

days.note: Nearly all parties do this route in a single long day from the Keep Kool (Twin Lakes Road) trailhead: hike the Yellow Aster Butte trail and drop to the Yellow Aster/Tomyhoi tarns, follow the boot path along Tomyhoi Ridge, then scramble the exposed final gully to the summit. The crux is a hard-snow traverse around a small moat below the false summit, followed by a steep class 3-4 gully to the true summit.
days.title: Car-to-car climb via Yellow Aster Butte

schedule.label: Leave Keep Kool trailhead
schedule.detail: Elev. ~3,150 ft on Twin Lakes Road; start on the Yellow Aster Butte trail.

schedule.label: Reach Yellow Aster/Tomyhoi tarns
schedule.detail: Drop off the main trail onto the boot path toward the Tomyhoi Arm and ridge crest.

schedule.label: Traverse the moat and final gully
schedule.detail: Crux hard-snow traverse around the moat below the false summit, then a long, loose, exposed class 3-4 gully/chimney to the true summit.

schedule.label: Summit
schedule.detail: 360-degree views to Baker, Shuksan, and into Canada; typical summit arrival 5-6 hours after starting.

schedule.label: Descend to trailhead
schedule.detail: Reverse the route; parties starting later or moving slower often finish the last stretch by headlamp.

days.objective: Summit Tomyhoi Peak and return to trailhead

itinerary.totalNote: A long single day: roughly 7.5-9 hours car-to-car, ~13-14 miles round trip with about 5,000-5,600 ft of gain and loss.

before.turnaround: Trip reports cite roughly 5–6 hours car-to-summit and about 5 hours back down from trailheads at 3,150–3,700 ft. Start early and set a firm turnaround time so the gendarme bypass and Class 3.5 slot aren't downclimbed in the dark or during afternoon thunderstorm buildup.

weather.typical: Typical North Cascades summer pattern - the Mt Baker/Nooksack area catches more moisture than ranges east of the crest, so expect a higher chance of clouds/showers than drier Cascade zones even in summer
weather.probability: Afternoon buildups and fast-moving frontal systems are possible even mid-summer; by September the chance of an early fall storm system increases, shrinking the reliable weather window

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Fall exposure is concentrated on the exposed summit block and along sections of the class 3-4 ridge crest - a slip there would be serious to fatal; loose rock on the ridge also creates rockfall risk to parties below

avalanche.zone: NWAC 'Mt Baker' zone is the nearest official forecast zone, but NWAC only issues forecasts roughly Nov-Apr - this route is climbed entirely outside the NWAC forecast season, so no active avalanche forecast applies during the July-September climbing window

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: No roped glacier travel on this route, but the approach passes near/below a small permanent snowfield (sometimes called the Tomyhoi Glacier); early-season snow bridges or moats near its edge warrant caution even though the route itself does not cross it

waypoints.name: Twin Lakes Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of high-clearance FS Road 3065 between the Twin Lakes; parking for ~20 vehicles, vault toilet, Northwest Forest Pass required at the self-issue kiosk.
waypoints.directions: Drive up Twin Lakes Road (FS-3065) to the trailhead between the two lakes. The final two miles are rough and one-lane in places; high clearance is recommended and four-wheel drive helps, though it isn't strictly required. Parking holds around 20 vehicles, with a vault toilet on site, and a Northwest Forest Pass is required at the self-issue kiosk. If your vehicle can't manage the last stretch, park at the Yellow Aster Butte trailhead instead and add about 2.5 miles of road walking each way.

waypoints.name: High Pass Trail (No. 676) junction
waypoints.note: Trail splits here; bear right/uphill onto Winchester Mountain Trail 685 while High Pass Trail continues north toward Mount Larrabee.
waypoints.directions: From the parking area between the two lakes, pick up Winchester Mountain Trail #685 heading north-northwest on moderately steep, well-graded tread through blueberry and heather. The signed junction comes up within the first quarter to half mile, while you are still among the last scattered trees.

waypoints.name: Unmarked snow-route junction
waypoints.note: Unofficial climbers' path splits off here for a steep direct scramble used as a snow shortcut early season; stay on the switchbacking main trail unless comfortable on steep snow.
waypoints.directions: Of the two branches, #685 is the one that switchbacks up toward the lookout; High Pass Trail #676 is the branch carrying on north toward Gargett Mine and Mount Larrabee. Above the sign the trail leaves the last trees for open, treeless southeast-facing slopes and climbs in tight switchbacks through fireweed and heather, with Twin Lakes, Tomyhoi Peak and Mount Baker opening up behind you. There is no water anywhere on this trail, so everything you drink comes from the car.

waypoints.name: Pass crest saddle
waypoints.note: Trail crests the ridge with open views toward Mount Larrabee and Tomyhoi Peak before switchbacking up the final push to the lookout.
waypoints.directions: The unmarked path splitting off here is a rougher, more direct scramble line up snow and scree. Unless you are set up for steep snow, ignore it and stay on the switchbacks, which are the standard and preferred line. They carry on up the open slope to where the trail crests the ridge just west and south of the summit, and the view swings around to Mount Larrabee, the Border Peaks and Tomyhoi.

waypoints.name: Narrow exposed trail sections
waypoints.note: Two narrow sections of trail with long drop-offs near the summit ridge require sure footing per the USFS trail description; can hold snow/ice well into July.
waypoints.directions: From the crest the trail turns along the ridge for the final few hundred feet of gain. Two short stretches through here are narrow with long drop-offs below and want sure footing; one is cut into rock. Steep snow can lie across this ground into July and in heavy years into August, and it hardens overnight, so an ice axe and comfort on firm snow are worth having early season.

waypoints.name: Winchester Mountain Lookout
waypoints.note: Historic 1935 fire lookout maintained by Mount Baker Hiking Club volunteers; 360-degree views of Mount Baker, Mount Shuksan, and Twin Lakes below.
waypoints.directions: Past the narrow sections it is a short, open walk along the ridge crest to the lookout. This is the same ground you reverse on the way down, and it is the stretch worth taking carefully if snow is lying: plunge-step or use the axe rather than trusting a boot-pack that has firmed up in the shade.

itinerary.cal: Twin Lakes Rd requires high clearance/4WD and may not open until mid-summer; steep snow near the saddle often lingers into July-August and warrants an ice axe.

days.note: A short, popular half-day trip from the Twin Lakes trailhead: climb through blueberry/fireweed slopes to a junction with the High Pass trail, cross a saddle, then finish the last steep 400 ft to the historic 1935 fire lookout. Most parties are up and back in 2.5-3 hours total, leaving plenty of time to explore nearby Winchester/High Pass or Tomyhoi views.
days.title: Car-to-car day hike to the lookout

schedule.label: Leave Twin Lakes trailhead (~5,200 ft)
schedule.detail: High-clearance/4WD needed for the final miles of Twin Lakes Rd; otherwise park near Yellow Aster Butte TH and add ~2.5 mi each way of road walking.

schedule.label: Pass High Pass trail junction
schedule.detail: Stay straight/right for Winchester; trail tightens into switchbacks through blueberries and fireweed.

schedule.label: Crest the saddle to the west side
schedule.detail: Views open up toward Mt Larrabee and the Border Peaks; steep snow can linger here into July/August and an ice axe is often warranted.

schedule.label: Reach Winchester Mountain Lookout (6,521 ft)
schedule.detail: 360-degree views of Baker, Shuksan, the Pickets, Larrabee, and Tomyhoi; lookout building itself keeps limited weekday hours if staffed.

schedule.label: Descend via same trail
schedule.detail: Reverse the ascent route back to the trailhead; total round trip commonly 2.5-3 hours for a fit party.

itinerary.totalNote: A short single-day outing: about 3.4 mi round trip, 1,300 ft gain, typically 2.5-3 hours car-to-car for a fit hiker.

weather.typical: Typical North Cascades summer pattern - warm, mostly dry days with the lookout perch and open traverse exposed to wind; the historic Mount Baker Hiking Club lookout offers minimal shelter
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms are possible but not the dominant risk here; wind exposure on the summit ridge is the more consistent factor

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Well-graded, maintained trail overall; the south/west-slope traverse has real fall exposure while it's still covered in steep, hardening snow (typically into July), and the access road itself is rough enough to be a stated hazard/deterrent

avalanche.zone: West Slopes North (NWAC winter/spring forecast zone covering the Mt Baker Highway area) - not an active NWAC forecast zone during the July-October climbing season for this route
